slides.title: Ends and Boundaries
slides.notes: Open by naming the chapter pivot: earlier invariants counted growth and measured hyperbolicity inside large balls, while this lecture asks what survives after the observer walks outside every bounded region. The three visual anchors are stable components, ray classes, and boundary maps that turn coarse maps into topological data.

slides.title: Boundary As A Functor
slides.notes: Use this slide to make the wish-list concrete. A useful boundary construction should assign a topological space to a metric space and should send a quasi-isometric embedding to a continuous boundary map. The important payoff is that quasi-isometries become homeomorphisms at infinity, so coarse geometry can be tested topologically.

slides.title: Ends Are Persistent Components
slides.notes: Define an end as the eventual component followed by a proper ray after bounded sets are removed. Students should watch the tails, not the starting point. Two rays represent the same end precisely when every bounded obstacle can be passed so that their far-out tails occupy the same remaining component.

slides.title: Three Model Spaces
slides.notes: Walk through the notebook diagnostic as a finite window into an eventual invariant. Removing a central ball separates the line into two directions, leaves the grid connected around the obstacle, and exposes many branches in the free tree. The displayed counts are local evidence, not a substitute for the limiting definition.

slides.title: Ends Of Groups
slides.notes: Emphasize that the group definition uses a Cayley graph only as a model. Changing finite generators changes the graph by quasi-isometry, so the space of ends is well defined up to canonical homeomorphism. The classification table then turns the number of ends into algebraic information about finiteness, virtual cyclicity, and splitting.

slides.title: Why Three Ends Cannot Occur
slides.notes: Present the proof idea visually rather than line by line. If a finitely generated group had a finite number of ends bigger than two, translates far along one ray would force two other far-out rays to pass near the origin after translation. Left invariance then contradicts their required separation outside the ball.

slides.title: Stallings Reads Branching Algebraically
slides.notes: Use Stallings' theorem as the bridge from coarse topology back to group structure. Infinitely many ends mean the large-scale geometry has genuine branching at infinity, and Bass-Serre theory packages that branching as an action on a tree with finite edge stabilizers. This is why ends are crude but powerful.

slides.title: Gromov Boundary Refines Ends
slides.notes: Contrast the two equivalence relations. Ends remember only which component a ray eventually occupies, while the Gromov boundary remembers a finite-Hausdorff-distance class of quasi-geodesic rays. In a one-ended hyperbolic space this can still leave a rich boundary, so the invariant sees more than component count.

slides.title: Hyperbolicity Makes Rays Rigid
slides.notes: The boundary definition is broad, but hyperbolicity is what makes it manageable. Morse stability says quasi-geodesic rays stay near geodesic rays, and properness lets one choose representatives from a common basepoint. Ask students to connect the disk picture with the previous chapter's thin-triangle technology.

slides.title: Free-Tree Prefix Cylinders
slides.notes: Tie the abstract boundary to the notebook's finite prefix calculation. A boundary point of a free group is an infinite reduced word, and a basic neighborhood fixes a finite prefix. The counts shown here, including 108 length-four prefixes and 27 per first letter, make Cantor-like branching inspectable.

slides.title: Boundary Maps Carry Quasi-Isometries
slides.notes: This is the technical engine behind the applications. A quasi-isometric embedding sends quasi-geodesic rays to quasi-geodesic rays, so it induces a boundary map. Finite-distance maps agree on the boundary, and a quasi-isometry gives a homeomorphism. This is how coarse equivalence becomes a topological obstruction.

slides.title: Boundaries Of Groups
slides.notes: Read the examples as a spectrum of how much infinity can remember. Finite groups have no boundary, the integers have two points, free groups have Cantor-set behavior, and closed hyperbolic n-manifold groups inherit a sphere. The contrast with ends explains why boundaries are the sharper invariant.

slides.title: Independent Boundary Points
slides.notes: Frame the mini Tits alternative as a boundary ping-pong argument. Infinite-order elements define two boundary points each. If two such pairs are disjoint, high powers push complementary domains back and forth, producing a free subgroup. If the pairs overlap, hyperbolicity forces the generated subgroup toward virtual cyclic behavior.

slides.title: Rigidity From Boundary Data
slides.notes: Mostow rigidity is the chapter's showcase for boundary methods. A homotopy equivalence between closed hyperbolic manifolds lifts to a quasi-isometry of hyperbolic space, hence to a sphere homeomorphism at infinity. In dimension at least three, the boundary map is forced to be conformal and therefore comes from an isometry.

slides.title: What The Invariant Can And Cannot See
slides.notes: Calibrate the method before the recap. Ends are stable and easy to compute but often collapse interesting spaces to one point of information. Gromov boundaries are much sharper for hyperbolic spaces, but outside the hyperbolic setting they can become too large or poorly behaved. The hypotheses matter.

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by returning to the chapter question: what can a group look like from infinitely far away? Ends answer with persistent components, Gromov boundaries answer with ray classes, and boundary functoriality turns quasi-isometries into maps of compact-looking spaces. The applications show why this is not just vocabulary.
